candidates.title: Clinical and Radiographic Outcomes of Suture Anchor Repair versus Transarticular Kirschner Wire Fixation of the Acromioclavicular Joint in Acute High-grade Dislocation: A Randomized Clinical Trial.
candidates.authors_short: Hirunthanawiwat T, Benjawongsathien K, et al.
candidates.journal: Journal of shoulder and elbow surgery
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: For high-grade acromioclavicular (AC) joint injury, repairing the AC ligament complex in addition to coracoclavicular (CC) stabilization provides superior biomechanical and functional outcomes. Rigid AC fixation, such as transarticular wires or hook plates, yields reliable outcomes but may be offset by complications. Therefore, this study compared the clinical and radiographic outcomes of an alternative AC stabilization with Suture anchor repair versus K-wire fixation. METHODS: A prospective randomized trial was conducted in 32 patients with acute AC dislocation. Patients were randomized (16 per group) to Suture anchor repair or transarticular K-wire fixation, both with the same nonbiologic CC suspensory technique. In the Suture anchor group, a single 2.8-mm anchor was inserted into the distal clavicle to repair the superior AC capsuloligamentous complex. The primary outcome was the Constant-Murley Score (CMS); secondary outcomes were the American Shoulder and Elbow Surgeons (ASES) and University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) shoulder scores, percentage coracoclavicular distance (%CCD) change, and complications, assessed at 4, 8, 16, 24, and 52 weeks. Repeated measurements were analyzed using multilevel Gaussian regression with Bonferroni adjustment, and differences were interpreted against published minimal clinically important difference thresholds. RESULTS: All 32 patients completed 52-week follow-up. The Suture anchor group included 3 Rockwood type IIIB and 13 type V, while the K-wire group included 8 type IIIB and 8 type V. The Suture anchor group had higher CMS at 4 weeks (mean difference, 12.7 points; 95% CI, 8.7-16.6), 8 weeks (7.9; 95% CI, 4.0-11.9), and 16 weeks (5.3; 95% CI, 1.4-9.3) (all P ≤ .003), with no difference at 24 or 52 weeks. ASES and UCLA scores were higher in the Suture anchor group at 4 and 8 weeks only (all P < .001). The K-wire group, after wire removal at 4 weeks, showed a smaller %CCD change at every interval, with a mean loss of 4.6% versus 14.5% at 52 weeks (mean difference, 9.9%; 95% CI, 3.4-16.4; P < .001). Complications occurred in 4 K-wire patients (25.0%; 4 pin migrations, 1 with superficial pin-tract infection) and in no Suture anchor patients (P = .101). CONCLUSION: While AC stabilization with suture anchor repair provided faster early functional recovery and K-wire fixation better maintained radiographic reduction, both techniques yielded comparable functional outcomes from 24 weeks and onward. Additionally, these findings should be limited to AC joint dislocation with primarily vertical instability, and the choice between techniques should be individualized. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I, Randomized Controlled Trial, Treatment Study.
candidates.score_reasoning: RCT comparing suture anchor vs K-wire fixation for AC joint dislocation in a high-impact shoulder journal with direct surgical decision-making implications, though limited by small sample size of 32 patients.
bullets: In a randomized trial of 32 patients with acute high-grade AC dislocation, suture anchor repair gave better shoulder function scores than K-wire fixation at 4 to 16 weeks, but both groups reached the same functional level by 24 weeks.
K-wire fixation maintained tighter radiographic reduction at one year, but 25% of K-wire patients had hardware complications including pin migration, compared to none in the suture anchor group.

For surgeons treating acute Rockwood type IIIB or V AC dislocations, suture anchor repair is a reasonable alternative to K-wire fixation, offering faster early recovery with fewer hardware complications at the cost of slightly less radiographic reduction.

candidates.title: Timing of platelet-rich plasma administration in arthroscopic rotator cuff repair: A systematic review and meta-analysis of randomised controlled trials.
candidates.authors_short: Tareen H, Mostafa OES, et al.
candidates.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
candidates.abstract: PURPOSE: Platelet-rich plasma (PRP) has been widely investigated as a biologic adjunct in arthroscopic rotator cuff repair (ARCR), yet clinical evidence remains heterogeneous. One potential source of variability is the timing of PRP administration, which may influence tendon-to-bone healing. This study aimed to evaluate the effect of PRP augmentation on structural healing and clinical outcomes following ARCR, with particular evaluation of outcomes according to the timing of PRP administration. METHODS: A systematic review was conducted in accordance with PRISMA guidelines and registered on PROSPERO. PubMed, Scopus, Cochrane CENTRAL and Web of Science were searched through 19 February 2026. Randomised controlled trials (RCTs) comparing PRP augmentation with control in adult patients undergoing ARCR were included. Trials were stratified by timing of PRP administration (intraoperative, post-operative-only or combined). The primary outcome was retears assessed by post-operative imaging at ≥6 months. Pooled risk ratios (RRs) with 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were calculated using a random-effects model. Heterogeneity was assessed using I2 statistics. RESULTS: Fifteen RCTs (1214 patients; 647 PRP and 567 control) met inclusion criteria. Overall, PRP administration at ≥6 months was associated with a reduced risk of retears (RR, 0.53; 95% CI, 0.40-0.70; p < 0.001; I2 = 0%). Subgroup analysis demonstrated that intraoperative PRP significantly reduced retear rates at ≥6 months (RR, 0.49; 95% CI, 0.35-0.68; p < 0.001; I2 = 0%) and ≥12 months (RR, 0.52; 95% CI, 0.30-0.91; p = 0.021; I2 = 0%). Post-operative-only PRP did not demonstrate a statistically significant reduction in retears (RR, 0.35; 95% CI, 0.01-8.12; p = 0.54). Absolute risk reduction at ≥6 months was approximately 12%, corresponding to a number needed to treat of 8. Functional outcome scores improved in both PRP and control groups, with significant differences between groups in included studies, but pooled analyses did not demonstrate consistent between-group differences. PRP was not associated with increased complication rates. CONCLUSION: Intraoperative PRP augmentation during ARCR is associated with a statistically significant reduction in retears. The limited post-operative-only PRP protocols do not demonstrate a comparable benefit and preclude a definitive conclusion that efficacy differs according to timing. These findings suggest a potential timing-dependent structural effect of PRP. However, structural improvements did not consistently translate into superior functional outcomes. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level I.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large registry-based prospective study (2563 cases) from Australia comparing knee osteotomy outcomes with conversion rates and direct comparison to UKR, highly relevant for joint preservation surgeons.
bullets: Intraoperative PRP during rotator cuff repair reduces retear rates by roughly half compared to controls, with a number needed to treat of 8.
PRP given only postoperatively showed no significant reduction in retears, suggesting timing of delivery matters for structural healing.
Despite lower retear rates with intraoperative PRP, functional outcome scores did not consistently improve over controls, so the clinical benefit remains structural rather than symptomatic.

candidates.title: Kaplan fiber tenodesis and anterolateral ligament reconstruction provide comparable functional outcomes after anterior cruciate ligament reconstruction: A propensity score-matched study at a minimum 2-year follow-up.
candidates.authors_short: Brossier C, Pintore A, et al.
candidates.journal: Knee surgery, sports traumatology, arthroscopy : official journal of the ESSKA
candidates.abstract: PURPOSE: Anterolateral augmentation is widely performed alongside anterior cruciate ligament (ACL) reconstruction to reduce residual rotational laxity and graft failure. Two strategies coexist: anterolateral ligament reconstruction (ALLR), using a free tendon graft, and lateral extra-articular tenodesis using the iliotibial band (ITB). Kaplan fibre tenodesis (KFT) uses the native ITB to reconstruct the distal Kaplan fibres at their anatomical femoral footprint. The purpose of this study was to compare functional outcomes and graft survival between these two anterolateral procedures. It was hypothesized that both techniques would provide equivalent functional outcomes at a minimum 2-year follow-up. METHODS: A retrospective comparative study was conducted using data from a prospective single-surgeon ACL reconstruction registry. Allocation to KFT or ALLR was determined intraoperatively by semitendinosus graft diameter. Propensity-score matching (1:1, nearest-neighbour) included age, sex, preoperative Tegner score, meniscal status and chondropathy, with exact matching on meniscal status. The primary outcome was functional outcome at a minimum 24-month follow-up, assessed with the Knee injury and Osteoarthritis Outcome Score (KOOS), the International Knee Documentation Committee (IKDC) subjective score, the Tegner activity scale and the Patient Acceptable Symptom State (PASS) for the IKDC, analyzed for equivalence using the two one-sided tests procedure with prespecified margins. Graft survival was secondary. RESULTS: Thirty-two pairs were matched from 106 eligible patients, with adequate covariate balance (all standardized mean differences < 0.13). Median follow-up was 44 months [interquartile range = 33-47] in the KFT group and 46 months [35-60] in the ALLR group. No significant difference was found for KOOS global (84.2 vs. 85.2; p = 0.153), IKDC (85.2 vs. 82.9; p = 0.176) or Tegner (7 vs. 7; p = 0.941). Equivalence was demonstrated for KOOS global (+5.21, 90% confidence interval [CI] = [+0.63 to +9.78]; p = 0.043) and Tegner (-0.06, 90% CI = [-0.88 to +0.76]; p = 0.031); for IKDC, the upper bound marginally exceeded the margin (+5.89, 90% CI = [+0.11 to +11.66]; p = 0.055). PASS-IKDC was reached by 27 of 32 (84.4%) versus 20 of 32 (62.5%) patients (p = 0.065). Graft re-rupture occurred in 2 of 43 KFT patients (4.7%) and 5 of 63 ALLR patients (7.9%) (log-rank p = 0.879). CONCLUSION: In patients undergoing primary ACL reconstruction, KFT provided functional outcomes equivalent to ALLR for the KOOS and Tegner scores at a minimum 2-year follow-up. Anterolateral stabilization can be achieved with an ITB-based technique at an anatomical femoral footprint, without a free tendon graft. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Level III, retrospective comparative study from a prospective cohort with propensity-score matching.
candidates.score_reasoning: Systematic review and meta-analysis of 15 RCTs examining PRP timing in rotator cuff repair with clinically actionable finding that intraoperative PRP significantly reduces retear rates.
bullets: In patients undergoing primary ACL reconstruction with anterolateral augmentation, Kaplan fiber tenodesis using the native ITB produced functional scores equivalent to anterolateral ligament reconstruction using a free tendon graft at two-year follow-up.
Graft re-rupture rates were low and similar between both techniques, at 4.7% for Kaplan fiber tenodesis and 7.9% for anterolateral ligament reconstruction.

Surgeons can achieve effective anterolateral rotational control without harvesting an additional tendon graft, preserving tissue and simplifying the procedure for indicated ACL reconstruction patients.

candidates.title: The Incidence of Late Periprosthetic Femoral Fractures by Implant Type-A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis.
candidates.authors_short: Brkljac M, Lovie J, et al.
candidates.journal: The Journal of the American Academy of Orthopaedic Surgeons
candidates.abstract: AIMS: Periprosthetic femoral fractures (PFF) are the leading cause of revision surgery after total hip arthroplasty when revision and fixation are combined, with morbidity and mortality akin to hip fractures. Polished taper slip (PTS) stems are increasingly seen as high risk; fracture risk of other cementation philosophies, or with noncemented stems excluding intraoperative or early postoperative fractures, remains uncertain. We compared the incidence of late PFFs (>3 months postoperatively) across different stem designs. METHODS: A systematic review of English-language studies published since 2000 was conducted. The Newcastle-Ottawa scale was used to assess study quality, with overall good ratings. A total of 28,854 hips from 27 studies were included (19,552 cemented, 9,302 noncemented). Stems were classified into subtypes to compare similar designs. Studies were excluded if early fractures (<3 months) could not be separated. RESULTS: No notable difference in late PFF risk was found between cemented and noncemented stems (incidence rate ratios: 1.00, 95% confidence interval 0.74 to 1.35). Among cemented stems, PTS designs had the highest fracture rate (0.15 per 100 person-years), markedly higher than French paradox (0.04), and composite beam stems (0.01) (P = 0.0158). Within PTS stems, CPT (0.53) and C stems (0.29) had the highest rates, whereas CPCS had the lowest (0.09). Within noncemented designs, type A stems did not show an advantage over type B (0.07 vs 0.12; P = 0.29). No difference in fracture rates between collared and noncollared noncemented implants was seen (P = 0.58 confidence interval 95% 0.53 to 1.42). CONCLUSION: Noncemented stems do not pose a higher late PFF risk than cemented stems. PTS stems show particularly high late fracture rates, with substantial variation between individual designs. By contrast, French paradox and composite beam stems appear protective and may offer a safer cemented option. No notable differences were observed among noncemented designs. Future studies should incorporate standardized methods for analyzing the relationship between the stem and femoral morphology.
candidates.score_reasoning: Systematic review and meta-analysis of nearly 29,000 hips directly addressing periprosthetic femoral fracture risk by implant type with strong clinical relevance for stem selection, particularly clarifying polished taper slip stem risk.
bullets: Polished taper slip cemented stems have the highest late periprosthetic femoral fracture rate, more than ten times higher than composite beam stems and roughly four times higher than French paradox stems.
Cemented and uncemented stems carry equivalent late fracture risk, so implant fixation method alone should not drive decision-making when trying to reduce periprosthetic fracture.
For surgeons using cemented stems, French paradox and composite beam designs appear to be safer choices than polished taper slip stems, particularly for patients already at fracture risk.

candidates.title: Intra-Articular Injection Into a Nonoperative Joint Within 90 Days Before Total Knee Arthroplasty is Associated With Increased Revision.
candidates.authors_short: Liao GY, Chansky H, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Intra-articular injections are commonly used to manage symptomatic osteoarthritis prior to total knee arthroplasty (TKA). While injections into the operative knee have been associated with increased postoperative infection risk when performed within three months of surgery, the effect of injections into nonoperative joints remains unclear. METHODS: We conducted a retrospective cohort study using a national all-payer administrative database of patients undergoing isolated primary TKA. The primary exposure was an intra-articular injection into a nonoperative joint within 90 days before surgery. Patients who had ipsilateral knee injections were excluded from the main analysis. The final cohort comprised 1,074,331 patients, of whom 5,419 (0.5%) received a nonoperative joint injection within 90 days before TKA. The primary outcome was all-cause revision at 90 days, six months, and one year. The secondary outcomes included etiology-specific revision. Multivariable Cox proportional hazards models were used to evaluate associations. RESULTS: Injection was associated with higher unadjusted revision rates at one year (1.25 versus 0.80%) and remained associated with increased revision hazard after adjustment at one year (hazard ratio [HR], 1.43) and six months (HR, 1.52), but not at 90 days. Etiology-specific analyses demonstrated that this association was primarily driven by periprosthetic joint infection (PJI), with increased hazard at one year (HR, 1.40). There were no consistent associations observed for mechanical loosening, instability, or periprosthetic fracture after adjustment. CONCLUSIONS: Intra-articular injection into a nonoperative, non-knee joint within 90 days before TKA was associated with an increased risk of revision, driven primarily by revision for PJI. These findings suggest that recent injection into a nonoperative, non-knee joint may be relevant to perioperative risk assessment, although the underlying mechanism remains uncertain.
candidates.score_reasoning: Large retrospective cohort study (1,074,331 patients) finding that contralateral joint injections within 90 days before TKA are associated with increased PJI-driven revision risk, with immediate and actionable perioperative implications.
bullets: Patients who received an intra-articular injection into any non-operative joint within 90 days before TKA had a 43% higher revision rate at one year, driven mainly by periprosthetic joint infection.
This risk applies to injections outside the operative knee, meaning even a hip, shoulder, or contralateral knee injection in the perioperative window may matter.
Surgeons should ask about recent injections into all joints, not just the operative knee, when counseling TKA patients on infection and revision risk.

candidates.title: Xa Inhibitors Are Associated with an Increased Risk of Manipulation after Primary Total Knee Arthroplasty Compared to Aspirin in a Contemporary Cohort.
candidates.authors_short: McGee AS, Baur AJ, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Aspirin is routinely used for venous thromboembolism prophylaxis following total knee arthroplasty (TKA), though some patients may require more aggressive chemoprophylaxis, now often with Xa inhibitors. There is concern Xa inhibitors may increase bleeding, leading to swelling and stiffness, which can lead to manipulation under anesthesia (MUA). This study compared rates of MUA following primary TKA for patients receiving Xa inhibitors versus aspirin and between Xa inhibitors in a contemporary cohort. METHODS: A database identified 435,789 patients undergoing unilateral primary TKA from 2021 to 2023. During the perioperative window (30 days preoperatively to 3 days postoperatively), 32,778 (7.5%) received rivaroxaban, 53,504 (12.3%) apixaban, and 349,507 (80.2%) aspirin. The incidence of MUA was determined using Current Procedural Terminology (CPT) code 27570 within 90 days following TKA. Univariable associations between chemoprophylaxis and MUA were assessed using Chi-square tests. Multivariable associations adjusted for patient demographics, Elixhauser Comorbidity Index, and body mass index were assessed using logistic regression with odds ratios (OR) and 95% confidence intervals (CI) reported. RESULTS: Overall, 13,142 (3.0%) underwent MUA, and this was more common in patients receiving Xa inhibitors versus aspirin (3.9 versus 2.8%, P < 0.001). After adjusting for patient characteristics, Xa inhibitors were associated with higher odds of MUA (OR, 1.60; 95% CI, 1.54 to 1.67). In univariable analysis, the rate of MUA was similar between rivaroxaban and apixaban (3.7 versus 3.9%, P = 0.11), though after adjusting for patient characteristics, rivaroxaban was associated with lower odds of MUA compared with apixaban (OR, 0.89; 95% CI, 0.83 to 0.95). CONCLUSION: Factor Xa inhibitors are associated with a significantly increased risk of MUA within 90 days of primary TKA compared to aspirin in a contemporary cohort. Unadjusted MUA rates were similar between rivaroxaban and apixaban. Adjusted odds were lower with rivaroxaban.
candidates.score_reasoning: RCT design (within-patient bilateral) with 48 patients providing high-quality evidence that patellar component downsizing increases patellofemoral crepitus, directly applicable to TKA surgical technique.
bullets: Patients receiving factor Xa inhibitors after primary total knee arthroplasty had 60% higher adjusted odds of requiring manipulation under anesthesia within 90 days compared to those on aspirin.
This applies to the growing subset of TKA patients deemed higher VTE risk and placed on rivaroxaban or apixaban instead of aspirin for perioperative prophylaxis.
When an Xa inhibitor is necessary, rivaroxaban carried modestly lower adjusted odds of manipulation than apixaban, though unadjusted rates were similar between the two agents.

candidates.title: Antibiotic Nails Outperform Implant Retention in Preventing Recurrent Infections After Intramedullary Nail Fixation of Tibial Shaft Fractures Complicated by Infection.
candidates.authors_short: Wilhelm ZC, Kommu K, et al.
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To compare infection recurrence rates between patients treated with antibiotic nail versus implant retention for open tibial shaft fractures initially treated with an intramedullary (IM) nail complicated by infection. METHODS: Design: Retrospective cohort study. SETTING: Level I trauma center. PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: Adults with tibial shaft fractures (OTA/AO 42A-C) treated with an IM nail between 2007 and 2023 who developed deep surgical site infections after index fixation were included. OUTCOME MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: The primary outcome was infection recurrence within 2 years requiring reoperation and antibiotics. Secondary outcomes included amputation rate, all-cause mortality rate, days in hospital within 1 year of index infection surgery, time to recurrence, and number of surgeries needed after recurrence. The association between treatment and the study outcomes was estimated using Cox proportional hazards models, controlling for potential confounders. RESULTS: A total of 96 patients were included, 75 (78%) [62 males; median age 47 years (interquartile range (IQR), 31 to 53)] were treated with conversion to antibiotic nail and 21 (22%) [18 males; median age 36 years (IQR, 27 to 48)] with implant retention. The antibiotic nail group was more likely to have chronic infections, requiring surgery 6 or more weeks after index IM nail fixation (65% vs. 38%, P = 0.03). The 2-year infection recurrence rate was significantly lower with implant removal and antibiotic nail (33%) than with implant retention (54%) (HR, 0.43; 95% CI, 0.20 to 0.92; P = 0.03). For the secondary outcomes collected, only the average number of surgeries required after recurrence differed significantly between the two groups, with 3.9 for antibiotic nail and 3.0 for implant retention (IRR, 1.39; 95% CI, 1.01 to 1.91; P = 0.04). CONCLUSIONS: Conversion to an antibiotic nail was associated with lower rates of infection recurrence compared with implant retention. The overall infection recurrence rates of 33% in the antibiotic nail cohort and 54% in the implant retention cohort highlight the challenges associated with treating infection after IM nail fixation of tibial shaft fractures, regardless of treatment strategy. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic, Level III.
candidates.score_reasoning: Secondary analysis of two RCTs addressing optimal timing of flap coverage in open fractures at 25 multinational institutions, directly relevant to orthopaedic trauma practice with strong study design pedigree.
bullets: In infected tibial IM nails, conversion to an antibiotic nail cut 2-year infection recurrence from 54% to 33% compared with keeping the original implant in place.
This applies to adult patients who develop deep infection after tibial shaft IM nailing, including those with chronic infections presenting more than 6 weeks out.
Antibiotic nail conversion is the preferred treatment for this complication, though one in three patients will still have recurrent infection requiring further surgery.

candidates.title: Nonoperative Management Deserves Consideration for Select Patients with Valgus-Impacted Femoral Neck Fractures.
candidates.journal: The Journal of bone and joint surgery. American volume
candidates.abstract: The valgus-impacted femoral neck fracture is unique among hip fractures. Patients are often relatively comfortable, and the fracture pattern is inherently more stable than other femoral neck fracture types. In situ fixation remains the default treatment for most surgeons, and this remains a reasonable approach, particularly for patients unable to reliably protect their weight-bearing. However, multiple randomized controlled trials and meta-analyses have revealed that, when surgery is chosen, arthroplasty carries a lower risk of reoperation and implant-related complications than fixation, with no difference in mortality. Additionally, nonoperative management has achieved rates of uneventful healing comparable with those of fixation in appropriately selected patients who were able to protect their weight-bearing, and delayed arthroplasty after failed nonoperative treatment has not been associated with excess morbidity compared with acute arthroplasty across measured outcomes. Given that fixation in situ may not have dramatically better efficacy than nonoperative care and that failed nonoperative management can be salvaged with delayed arthroplasty without excess morbidity, we propose that nonoperative management is a reasonable initial treatment for select patients. The best candidates are patients who are cognitively intact, living independently, and medically stable and who are reasonably comfortable and capable of mobilizing while protecting their weight-bearing. Close clinical and radiographic follow-up is required, with a low threshold for conversion to arthroplasty in the setting of uncontrolled pain, poor mobilization, or radiographic evidence of loss of reduction. Dementia, high comorbidity burden, and assisted living status are associated with failure of nonoperative management. In all circumstances, both fixation and acute arthroplasty remain valid alternative strategies. We advocate a shared decision-making approach that accounts for the risks and benefits of all treatment strategies as well as patient factors.
candidates.score_reasoning: High-prestige JBJS publication outlining the AJRR-C roadmap for registry-nested trials, highly relevant for surgeons engaged in arthroplasty research infrastructure and evidence-based practice advancement.
bullets: In cognitively intact, independent, medically stable patients with valgus-impacted femoral neck fractures, nonoperative management achieves healing rates comparable to in situ fixation when weight-bearing precautions can be reliably followed.
If nonoperative management fails, delayed arthroplasty carries no additional morbidity compared to acute arthroplasty, making it a viable salvage strategy.
Dementia, high comorbidity burden, and assisted living status predict failure of nonoperative management, and these patients should be directed toward fixation or arthroplasty upfront.

candidates.title: What Are the Long-term Outcomes of Periacetabular Osteotomy in a United States Cohort?
candidates.authors_short: Maroyan A, Mendola LC, et al.
candidates.abstract: BACKGROUND: Periacetabular osteotomy (PAO) is an effective and common hip-preserving procedure used to treat symptomatic acetabular dysplasia of the hip. Evidence regarding long-term outcomes after PAO remains limited. Information regarding long-term outcomes may be important in developing reasonable expectations for both patients and surgeons to facilitate effective therapeutic decision-making. QUESTIONS/PURPOSES: (1) What is the likelihood of long-term hip preservation and the level of pain at a minimum of 25 years of follow-up after PAO? (2) What clinical and radiographic factors were associated with patients having a poor result, which we defined either as having THA or a WOMAC score of ≥ 10 points at the most recent survey? (3) What were the outcome scores of patients who underwent THA after PAO, and how did these scores compare to the scores of the preserved hips and to the scores of age-related norms? METHODS: We retrospectively evaluated the cohort of the first 142 patients (171 hips) who underwent PAO performed by one surgeon to treat symptomatic dysplasia between 1991 and 1998. Twenty-three percent (33 of 142) of patients (37 hips) were lost to follow-up. This included six patients (6 hips) who had died, 23 patients (26 hips) who could not be located, and four patients (5 hips) who did not complete questionnaires. Seventy-seven percent (109 of 142) of eligible patients (134 hips) returned complete questionnaires at a median (range) of 27 years (25 to 33) after PAO. Our analyzed group included 87% female patients (95 patients, 117 hips) and 13% male patients (14 patients, 17 hips). The median (range) age at surgery was 25 years (9 to 45). The median (range) time of review after PAO was 27 years (25 to 33). The 53 hips that had undergone THA were reviewed at a median (range) of 11 years (1 to 28) after the THA. Kaplan-Meier analysis was used to assess survivorship free from conversion to THA. Hips were postoperatively evaluated using the pain subscale of the WOMAC index. We characterized a poor clinical outcome as either having a preserved hip with a WOMAC pain score of ≥ 10 or undergoing THA. All patients who were analyzed returned questionnaires; some were seen in person with images. Factors associated with a patient having a high (poor) WOMAC score for pain or undergoing THA were evaluated using a multinomial logistic regression model using generalized estimating equations. RESULTS: Of patients analyzed, 60% (81 of 134) of hips remained preserved. Forty percent (53 of 134) of hips had undergone THA at a median of 22 years after PAO. The survivorship free from conversion to THA at 25 years after PAO was 70% (95% confidence interval [CI] 62% to 78%), and the median (range) level of pain was 1 (0 to 20) of 20 points. After controlling for potentially confounding variables including sex, preoperative lateral center-edge angle and anterior center-edge angle, and postoperative lateral center-edge angle, we found that the following factors were associated with increased odds of having either a poor (≥ 10 points) WOMAC pain score or conversion to THA: preoperative joint space width ≤ 2 mm (HR 7.3 [95% CI 2.8 to 19.2]), labral tear noted intraoperatively (HR 2.8 [95% CI 1.3 to 5.8]), age at surgery > 21 years and < 35 years (HR 2.6 [95% CI 1.1 to 5.9]), and age at surgery ≥ 35 years (HR 3.4 [95% CI 1.1 to 11.0]). In patients who underwent THA, the median (range) WOMAC score was 1 (0 to 20) (lower scores represent less pain and better function), the median (range) modified Harris hip score was 85 (7 to 91) points (higher scores represent less pain and better function), and the median (range) HOOS pain score was 95 (0 to 100). The mean University of California, Los Angeles (UCLA) activity level score for the THA group was 6. In general, these scores did not differ by clinically important margins when compared with the hips that had not undergone THA or compared with age-related score norms. CONCLUSION: While a majority of hips can be preserved with good function at a mean of 27 years after PAO, our findings suggest that surgery should be considered as soon as the diagnosis of symptomatic dysplasia is made, given that older age at the time of surgery was independently associated with later THA or a WOMAC pain score of ≥ 10. If a patient develops painful arthrosis after a PAO, THA should be offered and expected to provide function comparable to age-related norms. Prospective registry-based multicenter studies of patients treated for symptomatic hip dysplasia are indicated to improve outcomes. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE LEVEL: III, therapeutic study.
candidates.score_reasoning: CORR publication on long-term PAO outcomes at minimum 25-year follow-up with 77% retention rate, providing rare and clinically valuable long-term data for hip preservation counseling.
bullets: At 27-year follow-up after periacetabular osteotomy for hip dysplasia, 70% of hips survived without conversion to total hip arthroplasty and preserved hips had near-zero median pain scores.

Narrowed preoperative joint space (2 mm or less), intraoperative labral tear, and older age at surgery (over 21 years) were each independently associated with worse outcomes or eventual total hip arthroplasty.

Patients who eventually required total hip arthroplasty after periacetabular osteotomy achieved pain and function scores comparable to age-matched norms, so conversion should be offered without hesitation when arthrosis becomes symptomatic.

candidates.title: Unplanned Reoperation and Patient-Reported Outcomes After Operative Treatment of Intraarticular Glenoid Fractures.
candidates.authors_short: McGlone PJ, Funk K, et al.
candidates.abstract: OBJECTIVES: To determine the proportion of patients undergoing unplanned reoperation and to report patient-reported outcomes after operative treatment of intraarticular glenoid fractures. METHODS: Design: Retrospective case series. SETTING: Single trauma institution. PATIENT SELECTION CRITERIA: Adults with operatively managed intraarticular glenoid fractures (OTA/AO 14F) from 2007 to 2024 were screened for eligibility. Patients were included if they had at least 182 days of clinical follow-up, at least 182 days of telephone follow-up, or underwent an unplanned reoperation within 182 days of the index surgery. OUTCOMES MEASURES AND COMPARISONS: The primary outcome was unplanned reoperation related to the glenoid injury. The secondary outcome was the SANE score, ranging from 0 (worst) to 100 (best). RESULTS: Fifty-four patients were included; mean age was 40 years (range, 20-73 years) and 74% were male. Twenty-six patients completed the SANE outcome assessment at a median of 9.3 years after surgery (IQR, 5.1-13.9 years; range, 0.6-21.9 years). The overall cohort had a median clinical follow-up duration of 7.7 months (IQR, 4.6-14.5 months; range, 0.4-77.9 months). Unplanned reoperation occurred in 15 of 54 patients (28%; 95% CI, 18%-41%). The median SANE score was 98 (IQR 76-100). CONCLUSIONS: In this case series of 54 patients, operative treatment of intraarticular glenoid fractures was associated with unplanned reoperation in 28% of patients. Twenty-six patients completed SANE outcome assessment at a median of 9.3 years after surgery, with a median score of 98. These findings suggest that operative fixation of intraarticular glenoid fractures can result in favorable patient-reported outcomes, although patients should be counseled regarding the possibility of reoperation. LEVEL OF EVIDENCE: Therapeutic, Level IV.
candidates.score_reasoning: Retrospective cohort at Level I trauma center showing antibiotic nails significantly outperform implant retention for infected tibial IMN fixation, with direct and immediately applicable surgical management implications.
bullets: After operative fixation of intraarticular glenoid fractures, 28% of patients required an unplanned reoperation.
Among patients followed nearly a decade out, median shoulder function scores were high, suggesting good long-term outcomes are achievable.
Counsel patients undergoing glenoid fracture fixation that reoperation is common, but functional recovery is generally favorable.
